 Taylor Sheridan Was ‘$330 Million Short’ When the 6666 Ranch Came Up, and Now He Admits There’s ‘No Playbook’
 by 
 Arden Lambert 
 Arden Lambert 
 Arden Lambert covers breaking country music news for Country Thang Daily. If it just happened in country music, Arden is on it.
 November 17, 2026 10:23 AM CST 
 Get Country Thang Daily first on Google Get CTD first on Google Add us as a preferred source in Top Stories Add us as a preferred source Add 
 Taylor Sheridan was thinking about retirement when the trustees of a Texas ranch asked if he wanted to buy it.
 He told Town & Country how that conversation went.
 “They said, ‘Do you want to pony up about 350 million bucks and take this place over?’ and I said, ‘Well, I’m $330 million short,'” he recalled.
 He made it happen anyway, and the Texas ranch has been in his hands since 2022. In a conversation with Yahoo Finance, Sheridan talked about how he has handled the Four Sixes so far and what he wants for it. One main goal is to make it a profitable business and hand it down to his son.
 “There is no playbook. We had ideas. The performance horse side, I knew extremely well,” he said.
 Taylor Sheridan Bought a Texas Ranch Burk Burnett Founded in 1870
 The ranch’s price tag has been reported at around $330 million, close to the “about 350 million bucks” the trustees mentioned to him. Sheridan raised the money through an overall deal with Paramount and by bringing in investors, and in 2022 he led that group in acquiring the ranch. He has since left Paramount. 
 The ranch came with a long history. Samuel “Burk” Burnett founded it in 1870 and named it for his 6666 cattle brand, according to Woman’s World, and it stayed in his family until his great-granddaughter, Anne Windfohr Marion, died in 2020.
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by 6666 Ranch (@6666ranch) 
 Sheridan told Parade at the time of the purchase that the ranch’s legacy and Miss Marion’s vision for it were vital to the rich heritage of ranching in Texas.
 Based in Guthrie, Texas, the ranch spans over 266,000 acres, twice the size of Chicago, and yet it is only the 9th-largest ranch in the state. It employs about 20 full-time cowboys plus 50 to 100 seasonal workers.
 Taylor Sheridan Is Building the Four Sixes Into a Business He Can Hand to His Son
 Taylor Sheridan came to the Four Sixes from a ranching life of his own. According to the ranch’s website, he grew up on a ranch in Cranfills Gap, Texas, and his Yellowstone money bought the 600-acre Bosque Ranch in 2019.

 He explained that he had been involved with performance horses for many, many years and knew how to make money from that side, and he has also opened the 6666 Granbury stallion station, a breeding facility for reining and herding horses. The cattle side, he said, could work in concept, but they had to find a lot of different partners.
 RELATED: Why Taylor Sheridan’s Wife, Nicole Sheridan, is Every Cowboy’s Dream 
 His plan for making it pay comes straight from his day job. “What I’ve always done is taken everything back to what I do for a living, which is I’m a storyteller. So let’s tell the story of the ranch and everything that we do. So the restaurant tells the story of the ranch, the events that we put on.”
 He is partnering with MGM Resorts on the Four Sixes Ranch Steakhouse at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas, and the 6666 will be featured in the upcoming season of Landman .
 Fiction is where he draws the line. On Dale Brisby’s Rodeo Time podcast, he said there will never be a TV show about the 6666 because he would never fictionalize it.
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by @reyzinthelimit_stallion 
 “There’s no fist fights, there’s no gun fights, there’s none of that nonsense. It’s just a boy comes here and learns how to be a man,” he said.
 “It’s a big responsibility, you know, to be the person who has to protect that brand. So…I have to be very, very careful with it,” he added.
 Burk Burnett’s family kept the 6666 brand for decades. Taylor Sheridan has had it for four, with no playbook to follow, and the goal he has named is a ranch that pays its own way by the time it goes to his son.
